title: Client Relationship Management

modules.title: Foundations: the client lifecycle, the client record and your starting point
modules.overview: You will see client relationship management as a cycle that runs from first enquiry to repeat order and referral, not a single sale. You will learn exactly what a useful client record contains, then audit how you keep client information today and pick a tool that suits your phone, data budget and number of clients.

lessons.title: The client lifecycle and why returning clients are worth more
objectives: Describe the five stages of the client lifecycle in your own words
Explain the difference between serving a client once and managing a relationship
Calculate a simple client lifetime value from your own prices
Identify the stage where your business loses most clients

blocks.text: **Client relationship management (CRM)** is the set of habits and records you use to look after people who already buy from you, so that they stay, buy again and recommend you. The word CRM is also used for software such as HubSpot or Zoho, but the habits come first. A tailor with a good notebook and a steady follow-up routine is doing CRM. A business with expensive software that nobody updates is not.

This course is for women who already have some clients: a caterer, a hairdresser, a tutor, a bookkeeper, a soap maker who supplies shops, a virtual assistant. If you are still learning how to talk to a new buyer, handle objections or recover from a complaint, the WODDI course **Customer Relations and Sales** covers that. Here we focus on what happens after the first sale: records, follow-ups, expectations, repeat orders and service history.

blocks.name: happy-customer
blocks.alt: A smiling customer holding a shopping bag next to a shop counter
blocks.caption: A client who comes back on her own is the clearest sign that the relationship, not just the product, is working.

blocks.text: The five stages of the client lifecycle

items: **Enquiry:** she asks a question, sees your Status, or is referred by a friend.
**Onboarding:** you agree what she is buying, the price, the deposit and the date. This is where expectations are set.
**Delivery:** you do the work or hand over the goods, and record what was delivered.
**After-care:** a short check that she is happy, a care tip, a thank-you. Most small businesses skip this stage.
**Repeat and referral:** she orders again, or sends someone to you. The cycle starts again, usually faster and with more trust.

blocks.title: The client lifecycle
items: Enquiry
Onboarding
Delivery
After-care
Repeat and referral
blocks.caption: Each loop round the cycle should be easier than the last, because you already know the client.

blocks.text: Look at where clients drop out. If many people enquire but few pay, your problem is earlier, in selling. If people buy once and disappear, the gap is usually after-care and follow-up, which is exactly what this course fixes.
Why a returning client is worth more

A new client costs you time and often money before she pays anything: answering questions, sending pictures, maybe paying for adverts or transport to meet her. A returning client already trusts your quality and your prices, so the conversation is shorter. She also tends to need fewer explanations, pays more readily and forgives a small delay because she knows your record. You do not need a published statistic to see this. Count it in your own business.

The simplest way to put a number on a relationship is **client lifetime value**: how much one client is likely to spend with you over the whole time she stays. The basic formula is: average order value multiplied by orders per year multiplied by the number of years she stays.

blocks.title: Worked example: lifetime value for a small chops caterer
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs a small chops business in Ibadan. Her average party order is about 25,000 naira (approximate). Her regular clients order about 3 times a year and typically stay with her for about 4 years.
steps: Average order value: 25,000 naira.
Orders per year: 3. So one year is 25,000 x 3 = 75,000 naira.
Years she stays: 4. So lifetime value is 75,000 x 4 = 300,000 naira.
Bisi notices that a one-time client is worth 25,000 naira, while a loyal client is worth about 300,000 naira, twelve times as much.
If one loyal client refers just one friend who behaves the same way, that single relationship has produced about 600,000 naira of business over four years.
blocks.result: Bisi decides that sending a thank-you message and a reminder before the festive season is worth far more than the few minutes it takes.

blocks.title: Use your own numbers
blocks.text: Lifetime value is an estimate, not a promise. Use real figures from your sales book or WhatsApp history. If you do not know how often clients reorder yet, that is the first thing your new records will tell you.
Transaction thinking versus relationship thinking

head: Situation
Transaction thinking
Relationship thinking
rows: Check she is happy three days later and note her feedback
Notice the gap in your records and send a useful message
She mentions her daughter's wedding in June
Write it in her record with a reminder for April
Record what was agreed so the next order is consistent

blocks.text: None of this needs a big budget. It needs a place to write things down, a routine for reading what you wrote, and the discipline to act on it. Over the next eleven lessons you will build exactly that.

takeaways: CRM is a set of habits and records first; software is optional.
The lifecycle has five stages: enquiry, onboarding, delivery, after-care, repeat and referral.
Lifetime value = average order x orders per year x years she stays.
Most small businesses lose repeat clients at the after-care stage.

activity.title: Find your lifetime value and your weakest stage
steps: Write down your average order value from your last ten sales.
Estimate how many times a year your regular clients order and how many years they have stayed.
Calculate your client lifetime value using the formula from this lesson.
Look at the five lifecycle stages and circle the one where you lose the most clients.
Write one sentence on why you think clients drop out at that stage.
activity.evidence: A note or photo of your lifetime value calculation and the stage you circled.

lessons.title: The client record: what to capture, and how to write useful context
objectives: List the core fields every client record needs
Write context notes that are specific, factual and useful later
Separate facts from opinions in what you record
Turn a conversation into a next action with a date

blocks.text: A **client record** is one entry per client that holds everything you would want to remember before you next speak to her. Without it, details live in your head and in long WhatsApp chats that you have to scroll through. Once you have more than about ten clients, memory starts to fail, and clients notice when you ask the same question twice or forget something they told you was important.
The core fields

head: Field
What to write
Why it matters
rows: Full name as she prefers it, WhatsApp number
Avoid calling her by the wrong name; reach her quickly
How she found you: referral (by whom), Status, market, Instagram
Shows which channels bring good clients; lets you thank referrers
Tells you how long the relationship has lasted
Date, item or service, amount paid
Shows reorder pattern and total spend
Sizes, styles, allergies she has told you, delivery times
Lets you get it right without asking again
Events she mentioned: shop anniversary, child's graduation, Christmas stock-up
Gives you a genuine reason to reach out
Anything you agreed: discount, free alteration, sample
Turns the record into a to-do list

blocks.name: card-index
blocks.alt: A box of index cards, one card per client
blocks.caption: Whether it is a card, a notebook page or a spreadsheet row, every client gets one record you can find in seconds.

blocks.text: Writing context notes that help

The most valuable field is often the free notes column, and it is also the one people fill badly. A good note is **specific, factual, dated and short**. It records what the client said or did, not your mood about her. Compare these:

head: Weak note
Useful note
rows: 12 Mar: ordered 3 ankara gowns for her shop. Sells mostly size 14 to 16.
2 Apr: asked twice for delivery before Friday. Prefers updates by voice note, not text.
20 May: niece's wedding 14 Sept, family aso ebi for about 30 people, colour not chosen yet.

blocks.text: Notice that words like "difficult" or "stingy" are opinions. They do not tell your future self what to do, and if a client ever saw your records they could cause offence. Record the behaviour instead: "asked for a 10 percent discount on two orders" is a fact you can plan around.
From conversation to next action

Every time you talk to a client, finish by asking yourself: what is the next thing I should do for this person, and when? Write it in the next action field. If there is genuinely nothing, write a check-in date based on her normal buying pattern. A record without a next action is just history; a record with one becomes a plan.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a chat into a record
blocks.context: For example, Amaka is a tailor in Enugu. A new client, Chioma, sends voice notes on 3 June asking for two office dresses. During the chat Chioma mentions she was referred by Nkechi, that she starts a new job on 1 July, and that she dislikes sleeveless styles.
steps: Name and phone: Chioma, her WhatsApp number.
Source: referral by Nkechi. Amaka adds a note to thank Nkechi.
First order: 3 June, 2 office dresses, 36,000 naira (approximate) agreed, 18,000 naira deposit paid.
Preferences: no sleeveless; prefers knee length; voice notes rather than calls.
Important date: new job starts 1 July.
Promises made: dresses ready by 24 June, one free adjustment within two weeks.
Next action: send fitting reminder on 20 June.
blocks.result: In two minutes Amaka has a record that tells her exactly what to do next and gives her a natural reason to message Chioma in July to ask how the new job is going.

blocks.title: Write it the same day
blocks.text: Update the record within 24 hours of any order, delivery or meaningful conversation. After a week you will have forgotten the small details, and the small details are what make clients feel remembered.

blocks.title: A complete client record
items: Name, phone, source
Order history with amounts
Preferences and important dates
Promises made
Next action with date
blocks.caption: If any of these five are missing, the record will not help you act.

blocks.text: Where the details come from

You rarely get these details in one go. Preferences appear in passing ("last time the sleeves were a bit tight"), important dates come up in small talk, and the source often comes from the first message ("Nkechi gave me your number"). Get into the habit of reading back over a chat after an order is closed and pulling out anything worth keeping. Five minutes per client, done once, saves you from scrolling through months of messages later. If a detail is unclear, ask a simple question next time you speak rather than guessing.

blocks.title: Only what you need
blocks.text: Do not record things that have nothing to do with serving her, such as her religion, health details she did not share for the order, or gossip from other clients. Keep what helps you serve her well, and nothing more. Lesson 8 covers client data privacy in detail.

takeaways: One record per client, with the same core fields every time.
Good notes are specific, factual, dated and short; avoid opinions.
Every record should end with a next action and a date.
Update records within 24 hours while details are fresh.

activity.title: Write three full client records
steps: Choose your three most recent clients.
For each, fill in all eight core fields from the table, using your chat history to find dates and amounts.
Rewrite any opinion words as factual behaviour.
Give each client a next action and a date in the next 30 days.
Check that nothing in the records is unnecessary or private beyond what the order needed.
activity.evidence: A photo of the three records in your notebook, or a screenshot of them in your phone.

lessons.title: Auditing your current system and choosing the right tool
objectives: Score your current client management habits honestly
Compare a notebook, Google Sheets, WhatsApp Business labels and a free CRM app
Choose a tool that matches your client numbers, phone and data budget
Protect your client information with basic phone and account security

blocks.text: Before you build anything, look honestly at what you do now. Many women in business keep client details in four places at once: saved contacts, WhatsApp chats, a sales notebook and their memory. Nothing connects them, so follow-ups depend on luck. A short audit shows where the gaps are.
A ten-point self-audit
Answer yes or no to each statement. Give yourself one point for every yes.

items: I can find any client's phone number in under 30 seconds.
I can say how many orders my top five clients made last year.
I know which clients have not bought for three months or more.
I write down client preferences, not just orders.
I record every promise I make (discounts, free extras, dates).
I contact some clients when I am not trying to sell anything.
I check on clients a few days after delivery.
I know which clients came from referrals, and from whom.
My client information would survive if my phone was lost tomorrow.
I spend a fixed time each week reviewing my clients.

blocks.text: A score of 0 to 3 means you are relying almost entirely on memory. A score of 4 to 7 means you have some good habits but they are not joined up. A score of 8 to 10 means you need refining, not rebuilding. Whatever your score, write it down: you will re-take this audit at the end of the course to measure your progress.

blocks.name: filing-system
blocks.alt: A woman organising folders into a filing cabinet
blocks.caption: Choosing one home for client information is the first step to stop details getting lost across chats and notebooks.

head: Tool
Good for
Limits
Cost

Hard to search or sort; lost if the book is lost; no reminders
15 to a few hundred clients; sorting, filtering, totals; free backup to Google Drive

Tagging chats by stage such as New order or Pending payment

blocks.text: For most women on this course the best combination is **Google Sheets as the main record plus WhatsApp Business labels for daily chat organisation**. The sheet holds history and next actions; the labels let you see at a glance which chats need attention today. Module 2 shows you how to build both.

blocks.title: Notebook or spreadsheet?
items: Paper notebook
Google Sheets
left: Lost if the book is lost
right: Backed up to your Google account
Needs data and a Google account
blocks.caption: A notebook is fine to start; move to a spreadsheet once you pass about 15 regular clients.

blocks.title: Worked example: an audit and a tool decision
blocks.context: For example, Funmi sells liquid soap and disinfectant in 4-litre kegs to about 40 households and 6 small shops in Abeokuta. She uses an Android phone and buys a monthly data bundle.
steps: She scores the audit: yes on questions 1, 4 and 7 only. Score: 3 out of 10.
Her biggest gaps: she does not know who has stopped buying, and her records would not survive a lost phone.
She has 46 clients, well above the 15 where a notebook becomes hard to manage.
She chooses Google Sheets because it is free, works on her phone, and backs up to her Google account automatically.
She also switches from ordinary WhatsApp to WhatsApp Business so she can label chats. WhatsApp offers a way to move to the Business app on the same number.
blocks.result: Funmi has a clear starting score of 3, a reason for each choice, and a plan to build her sheet in Module 2.

blocks.text: Whatever you choose, keep one tool as the single home for client records. Copies scattered across a notebook, the sheet and your contacts soon disagree, and then you cannot trust any of them. If you start on paper, plan the date you will move to a spreadsheet.

blocks.title: Protect the phone that holds your clients
blocks.text: Your client list is valuable and private. Set a screen lock (PIN, pattern or fingerprint). Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp (Settings, Account, Two-step verification) so no one can register your number on another phone. Use a strong password on your Google account and turn on Google's 2-Step Verification. Never share a WhatsApp or SMS verification code with anyone, even someone claiming to be from WhatsApp or your bank.

blocks.title: Saving data
blocks.text: Google Sheets can work offline on Android if you turn on offline access for the file in the Sheets app. You can update records during the day without data and let them sync later on Wi-Fi or when your bundle is active.

takeaways: Audit before you build; write down your score to measure progress later.
A notebook works for a handful of clients; Google Sheets is the best free step up.
WhatsApp Business labels organise chats but are not a full client record.
Secure your phone, WhatsApp and Google account before storing client data.

activity.title: Audit and decide
steps: Take the ten-point audit and write your score with today's date.
Count your current active clients.
Choose your main tool and write one sentence explaining why.
Turn on a screen lock, WhatsApp two-step verification and Google 2-Step Verification if not already on.
Write one relationship you want to strengthen during this course and why.
activity.evidence: A dated note with your audit score, client count, tool choice and the relationship you chose.

quiz.q: Kemi's clients usually spend about 10,000 naira per order, order 6 times a year and stay about 2 years. What is her estimated client lifetime value?
quiz.explain: 10,000 x 6 = 60,000 per year, and 60,000 x 2 years = 120,000 naira.

quiz.q: Many people buy from Grace once but very few come back. Which lifecycle stage should she strengthen first?
quiz.explain: If people buy once and disappear, the gap is after delivery: after-care and follow-up lead to repeat orders.

quiz.q: Which client note is the most useful?
options: 10 Aug: ordered 50 packs for her shop opening on 2 Sept; prefers delivery before 10am
quiz.explain: Useful notes are specific, factual and dated, and they tell you what to do next.

quiz.q: Funmi has 46 regular clients and a smartphone with a small data bundle. Which main tool fits her best?
options: Google Sheets, with WhatsApp Business labels for daily chats
A paid CRM designed for large sales teams
quiz.explain: Google Sheets is free, sortable and backed up, and labels help her manage chats. Labels alone cannot hold order history.

quiz.q: Someone calls Ada saying he is from WhatsApp and asks for the 6-digit code just sent to her phone. What should she do?
options: Give the code so her account is verified
Send it by text instead of reading it aloud
Refuse, never share the code, and make sure two-step verification is on
quiz.explain: Verification codes let someone take over your account and your client chats. Never share them; two-step verification adds protection.

quiz.q: What should every client record end with?
options: A next action and a date
quiz.explain: A next action with a date turns a record into a plan. Personal details unrelated to the order should not be stored.

modules.title: Guided practice: tracker, follow-up rhythm and feedback
modules.overview: You will build a working client tracker in Google Sheets with an order log, automatic totals and an overdue highlight. Then you will set clear expectations at onboarding, plan follow-ups and repeat-order reminders from each client's real buying pattern, and learn to read the signals that show whether a relationship is healthy.

lessons.title: Building your client tracker in Google Sheets
objectives: Set up a Clients tab and an Orders tab with the right columns
Add drop-down lists so status is always written the same way
Use COUNTIF and SUMIF to count orders and total spend per client
Highlight overdue follow-ups automatically with conditional formatting

blocks.text: In this lesson you build the tool you will use for the rest of the course. It has two tabs. **Clients** has one row per person, with her details and next action. **Orders** has one row per order, so a client who has bought eight times has eight rows there. Keeping orders separate means you never squeeze history into one cell, and Sheets can add it up for you.
Step 1: create the two tabs

items: Open the Google Sheets app or sheets.google.com and create a blank spreadsheet. Name it "Client tracker".
Rename the first tab "Clients". Add a second tab and name it "Orders".
In Clients, row 1, type these headings from column A to J: Client, Phone, Source, First order, Preferences, Important dates, Promises, Status, Next action, Next action date.
Add two more headings in K and L: Orders, Total spent. These will fill themselves.
In Orders, row 1, type: Date, Client, Item or service, Amount, Paid, Notes.
Freeze row 1 on both tabs (View, Freeze, 1 row) so the headings stay visible as you scroll.

blocks.name: spreadsheets
blocks.alt: A woman working on a large spreadsheet on screen
blocks.caption: Two simple tabs, Clients and Orders, are enough to give you a real client history.

blocks.text: Step 2: drop-down lists for consistency

If you sometimes type "active", sometimes "Active client" and sometimes "regular", you cannot filter properly. Fix this with **data validation**. Select column H in Clients, then choose Data, Data validation, add a rule, and pick "Dropdown". Enter the options: New, Active, Quiet, Lapsed. Do the same for the Client column in Orders using "Dropdown (from a range)" pointing at Clients!A2:A, so every order is linked to a client name spelled exactly the same way.

head: Status
Meaning (choose your own time limits)
rows: First order in the last 30 days
Ordered within her normal reorder gap
Past her normal gap but under twice the gap
No order for more than twice her normal gap

blocks.text: Step 3: let Sheets count and add

In Clients, cell K2, type =COUNTIF(Orders!B:B,A2). This counts how many rows in the Orders tab have this client's name. In L2 type =SUMIF(Orders!B:B,A2,Orders!D:D). This adds up the amounts for her orders only. Drag both cells down to the last client row. Now every new order you log updates her totals automatically.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking the formulas by hand
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a home bakery in Port Harcourt. Her Orders tab has four rows for her client Ifeoma: 5 Jan 18,000 naira, 14 Feb 22,000 naira, 2 Apr 18,000 naira and 30 May 25,000 naira (all approximate).
steps: COUNTIF looks for "Ifeoma" in column B of Orders and finds 4 rows, so K shows 4.
SUMIF adds the matching amounts: 18,000 + 22,000 + 18,000 + 25,000 = 83,000.
Ngozi checks with a calculator and gets 83,000 naira, the same as cell L.
She notices one order was typed as "Ifeoma " with a space. COUNTIF missed it until she fixed the spelling, which is why the drop-down list matters.
blocks.result: Ngozi trusts her totals because she tested them once by hand, and she now sees Ifeoma is one of her highest-spending clients.

blocks.text: Step 4: highlight overdue follow-ups

Select the range A2:L in Clients. Choose Format, Conditional formatting, and under "Format cells if" pick "Custom formula is". Type =AND($J2<>"",$J2<TODAY()) and choose a light red fill. Any client whose next action date has passed now turns red. Each morning, the red rows are your follow-up list for the day.

blocks.title: How the tracker works daily
items: Log order in Orders
Totals update automatically
Set next action date
Red row when overdue
Act, then update
blocks.caption: One order line and one date are all you type; the sheet does the counting and reminding.

blocks.text: Common mistakes and quick fixes

items: **Dates typed as text:** if you type 3/6 in one row and June 3 in another, Sheets may not recognise both as dates, and the overdue highlight will fail. Select the date columns and choose Format, Number, Date so every entry is stored the same way.
**Amounts with the naira sign or commas typed in:** type 18000, not N18,000. Then use Format, Number to display it nicely. Text amounts are ignored by SUMIF.
**One client, two rows:** search the Client column before adding a new name. If a client appears twice, merge her orders under one spelling and delete the extra row.
**Formulas not copied down:** new clients added at the bottom need the COUNTIF and SUMIF formulas too. Drag the formulas a few hundred rows down in advance so they are ready.

blocks.title: Filter instead of scrolling
blocks.text: Turn on a filter (Data, Create a filter) so you can show only Quiet clients, or sort by Total spent to see your top ten. On a phone, filter views keep things readable on a small screen.

blocks.title: Keep the sheet private
blocks.text: Check the Share button: the file should be shared with no one, or only with a trusted staff member using their own Google account. Never set it to "Anyone with the link", because client phone numbers would then be visible to anyone who gets the link.

takeaways: Use two tabs: one row per client, one row per order.
Drop-down lists keep names and statuses spelled the same way.
COUNTIF and SUMIF give order count and total spend per client.
Conditional formatting turns overdue follow-ups red each day.

Add the Status drop-down and link the Orders client column to the client list.
Enter at least 10 real clients and all their orders you can find in the last six months.
