lessons.title: Setting expectations, follow-up rhythms and repeat-order reminders
objectives: Write a clear order confirmation that sets expectations in writing
Plan a follow-up sequence from confirmation to after-care
Calculate a client's typical reorder gap from her order dates
Use WhatsApp Business labels and quick replies to keep follow-ups on track

blocks.text: Many relationship problems start before delivery, when the client and the business understood different things. One thought "Friday" meant morning; the other meant evening. One thought the price included delivery; the other did not. A short written **order confirmation** prevents most of these arguments and gives you a record to refer back to.
The order confirmation
Send it as a WhatsApp message once the client agrees, and ask her to reply "confirmed". It should state:

items: What exactly she is getting (quantity, size, colour, scope of the service).
The total price, what it includes, and what it does not include (for example delivery).
Deposit amount and when the balance is due.
Delivery or completion date and time window.
What happens if she changes her mind or wants changes (for example one free adjustment within 7 days).
How and when you will update her.

blocks.title: Confirm payments in your bank app
blocks.text: Before marking an order as Paid in your tracker, check that the money has actually arrived in your bank or wallet app (for example Opay, Moniepoint or your bank). Fake transfer screenshots and fake SMS alerts are common scams. A screenshot is not proof of payment.
A follow-up sequence after every order

blocks.title: Follow-up timeline for one order
items: Day 0: confirmation
Before delivery: progress update
Delivery day: handover note
Day 3: after-care check
Reorder point: reminder
blocks.caption: Five touches spread across the order give the client confidence without crowding her.

blocks.text: The after-care check is a short, specific message: "Good afternoon Mrs Okafor, I hope the trays went well at the meeting. Was the quantity right for your guests?" It shows you care about the result, not just the payment, and it often brings out feedback or a new order. Record her answer in the Notes column.
Working out when she will need you again

Many products and services repeat on a natural cycle: hair is redone every few weeks, a shop restocks every month, a child's lesson fees are due each term. Your Orders tab already shows each client's cycle. The **reorder gap** is the average number of days between her orders. To find it, take the days between her first and last order and divide by the number of gaps (one less than the number of orders).

blocks.title: Worked example: a reorder reminder for a shop client
blocks.context: For example, Funmi supplies 4-litre kegs of liquid soap to Halima, who runs a provisions shop. Halima's orders were on 3 Feb, 1 Mar, 4 Apr and 2 May.
steps: Days from 3 Feb to 2 May: 25 days left in February, plus 31 in March, 30 in April and 2 in May = 88 days.
Halima has 4 orders, so 3 gaps. 88 divided by 3 is about 29 days.
Funmi sets the reminder a few days before the gap ends: 2 May plus 26 days is 28 May.
On 28 May she messages: "Good morning Halima, your last soap delivery was 2 May. Shall I bring the usual 6 kegs on Friday?"
If no order comes within twice the gap (about 58 days), Halima's status becomes Quiet, then Lapsed, and Funmi plans a different kind of check-in.
blocks.result: Halima is reminded before she runs out, so she does not buy from another supplier just because Funmi was not there at the right moment.

blocks.name: reminders
blocks.alt: A phone screen with reminder notifications
blocks.caption: A reminder timed from her own buying pattern feels like good service, not pressure.

blocks.text: WhatsApp Business tools that help

The WhatsApp Business app comes with default **labels** such as New customer, New order, Pending payment, Paid and Order complete, and you can add your own, for example "After-care due" or "Reorder soon". Long-press a chat to add a label, then use the chat filter to see all chats with that label. **Quick replies** let you save a message you send often, such as your order confirmation, and insert it by typing a forward slash and a shortcut word. Always personalise the name and details before sending.
Keeping the confirmation short and friendly

A confirmation does not need to sound like a legal contract. Six short lines are enough. Here is an example a tailor might send: "Thank you Chioma. Confirming: 2 office dresses, knee length, sleeves, fabric supplied by you. Total 36,000 naira, deposit 18,000 received, balance on collection. Ready Tuesday 24 June after 2pm. One free adjustment within 7 days. I will send you a photo when they are ready. Please reply 'confirmed'." Save a version like this as a quick reply and change the details each time. When the client replies, you have a clear written record of what both of you agreed, which you can point to calmly if there is ever a disagreement about price, date or style.

blocks.title: How often is too often?
blocks.text: A useful rule: one message per stage of an order, and between orders, no more than one non-sales message a month unless the client starts the conversation. Watch her replies: short or no replies over several messages mean you should space them out.

takeaways: A written order confirmation prevents most misunderstandings.
Follow each order with a progress update, handover note and day-3 after-care check.
Reorder gap = days between first and last order divided by number of gaps.
Check payments in your bank app, never by screenshot.

activity.title: Set up your follow-up rhythm
steps: Write your own order confirmation template and save it as a WhatsApp Business quick reply.
Create two custom labels: After-care due and Reorder soon.
Calculate the reorder gap for three clients with at least three orders each.
Set a next action date in your tracker for each of them, a few days before the gap ends.
Send one after-care check to a client who received an order in the last week and record her reply.
activity.evidence: Your confirmation template, the three reorder gap calculations, and a screenshot of one after-care message (with the client's number hidden).

lessons.title: Reading relationship signals and asking for feedback
objectives: Recognise early warning signs and healthy signs in a client relationship
Ask for feedback with two or three well-chosen questions
Calculate a simple Net Promoter Score from client answers
Adjust your contact style based on what clients tell you

blocks.text: Clients rarely announce that they are leaving. They just order less, reply more slowly, and one day you realise you have not heard from them for months. Your tracker helps you see these patterns early, while there is still time to ask what has changed.
Signals to watch

head: Healthy signals
Warning signals
rows: Orders arrive within her usual reorder gap
Gap is getting longer each time
Replies to your messages, sometimes chats
Reads but does not reply to several messages
Refers friends, mentions you on Status
Asks for discounts she never asked for before

blocks.text: A single warning sign may mean nothing: people travel, fall ill or run short of money. Two or more together are worth a gentle, honest check-in. Do not guilt her for not buying. Ask whether your service still fits her needs.

blocks.name: customer-survey
blocks.alt: A person filling in a short survey form on a large screen
blocks.caption: A short, well-timed feedback question tells you more than guessing from silence.

blocks.text: Asking for feedback

Ask after a completed order, or every few months for regular clients. Keep it to two or three questions so it takes under a minute. You can ask directly in WhatsApp or make a free Google Form and send the link. Good questions are specific and open:

items: "What is one thing I do that you would not want me to change?"
"What is one thing that would make ordering from me easier?"
"On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend me to a friend?"

blocks.text: The last question is the basis of the **Net Promoter Score (NPS)**, a widely used measure created by Fred Reichheld and Bain and Company. Clients who answer 9 or 10 are **promoters**, 7 or 8 are **passives**, and 0 to 6 are **detractors**. NPS is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors. It ranges from minus 100 to plus 100.

blocks.title: Worked example: calculating NPS for a tutoring service
blocks.context: For example, Ruth runs home lessons for primary school pupils in Lagos and asks 20 parents the 0 to 10 question at the end of term.
steps: 12 parents answer 9 or 10: promoters. 12 out of 20 is 60 percent.
5 parents answer 7 or 8: passives. They are not used in the formula.
3 parents answer 6 or lower: detractors. 3 out of 20 is 15 percent.
NPS = 60 minus 15 = 45.
Ruth reads the written answers from the three detractors. Two mention that lesson times changed without notice.
blocks.result: Ruth's score is 45, and more importantly she has a specific fix: give parents at least a week's notice of any schedule change, and write this rule into her confirmation message.

blocks.title: Small numbers move a lot
blocks.text: With only 20 answers, one parent changing from 6 to 9 moves NPS by 15 points. Treat the score as a rough guide and track it over time. The written comments are usually more useful than the number.

blocks.title: From signal to better service
items: Notice a signal
Ask a short question
Listen without defending
Change one thing
Record and recheck
blocks.caption: Feedback only helps when it leads to one specific change you can check later.

blocks.text: Adjusting your contact style

Feedback also tells you how each client likes to be contacted. Some prefer voice notes, some text, some a call. Some like monthly updates; others only want to hear from you when their order is ready. Write the preference in her record and respect it. A client who asked for fewer messages and still gets weekly broadcasts will mute you, and then even your important messages will be missed.
Making the feedback form

items: Open forms.google.com (or the Google Forms option inside Google Drive) and start a blank form.
Add the 0 to 10 question using the Linear scale question type, from 0 to 10.
Add the two open questions as Paragraph questions, and make them optional so clients can answer only the scale if they are busy.
Do not ask for phone numbers or names unless you need to follow up; anonymous answers are often more honest.
Press Send, choose the link option, shorten the URL and paste it into a WhatsApp message.
Open the Responses tab to see answers, or link them to a sheet to calculate your NPS.

blocks.text: Send the link with a short personal line, not on its own: "Thank you for this term. Would you answer 3 quick questions to help me improve? It takes one minute." Expect that only some clients will reply, and do not chase anyone more than once.

blocks.title: Thank people for criticism
blocks.text: When someone points out a problem, thank her, tell her what you will change, and later tell her you changed it. Clients who see their feedback acted on often become your strongest supporters.

takeaways: Watch for longer gaps, smaller orders and unanswered messages.
Ask two or three short, specific feedback questions.
NPS = percentage of promoters (9 to 10) minus percentage of detractors (0 to 6).
Act on one specific change and tell the client you made it.

activity.title: Run a mini feedback round
steps: Filter your tracker for clients whose gap is getting longer, and list any with two or more warning signals.
Send a short, honest check-in to one of them and record her reply.
Send the three feedback questions to at least five recent clients.
Calculate your NPS from the answers you receive.
Choose one change based on the comments and note when you will tell clients about it.
activity.evidence: A sheet or note showing the answers, your NPS calculation and the one change you chose.

quiz.q: A client ordered on 1 March, 31 March and 30 April. What is her approximate reorder gap?
quiz.explain: 1 March to 30 April is 60 days across 2 gaps, so about 30 days between orders.

quiz.q: In Google Sheets, which formula counts how many orders in the Orders tab belong to the client named in A2?
quiz.explain: COUNTIF counts rows where column B matches the name in A2. SUMIF adds up amounts instead.

quiz.q: A client sends a screenshot of a bank transfer for her balance. What should you do before marking the order Paid?
options: Mark it paid; the screenshot is enough
Check that the money has arrived in your own bank or wallet app
Ask her to send the screenshot again
quiz.explain: Fake screenshots and fake alerts are common. Only money showing in your own account confirms payment.

quiz.q: Out of 10 clients, 6 answer 9 or 10, 2 answer 7 or 8, and 2 answer 5. What is the NPS?
quiz.explain: Promoters 60 percent minus detractors 20 percent equals 40. Passives are not counted.

quiz.q: Which detail most belongs in a written order confirmation?
options: The delivery date and what the price includes
A long story about your business
Your personal opinions about her style
quiz.explain: The confirmation sets expectations: item, price, inclusions, deposit, date and change policy.

quiz.q: Why use a drop-down list for the Client column in your Orders tab?
options: It stops other people opening the sheet
Names are spelled exactly the same, so COUNTIF and SUMIF find every order
quiz.explain: A small spelling difference, even an extra space, makes the formulas miss orders. Drop-downs prevent this.

modules.title: Quality and evidence: service records, privacy and retention numbers
modules.overview: You will set a quality standard for your records and run a monthly account review that sorts clients into four groups with a clear action for each. You will learn how Nigeria's data protection law applies to a small client list, how to stay honest about capacity, and how to measure repeat rate, retention, churn and referrals from your own tracker.

lessons.title: Service records, the promises log and the monthly account review
objectives: Apply a written quality standard to your client records
Keep a promises log so no commitment is forgotten
Sort clients into four groups using value and engagement
Run a 30-minute monthly account review with a clear action for each client

blocks.text: A tracker is only as good as the information in it. Out-of-date records are dangerous because they look reliable: you may send a reorder reminder to a client who told you last month she has closed her shop. This lesson gives you a simple standard, a way to keep promises visible, and a monthly routine to look at all your clients together rather than one chat at a time.
A five-point record standard

items: Every order is logged in the Orders tab within 24 hours.
Every client has a status and a next action date; none are blank.
Notes are dated and factual, with no opinion words.
Any promise (discount, free service, date) is logged the day it is made.
Clients who ask to stop hearing from you are marked and never messaged for marketing again.

blocks.text: Check yourself once a month by filtering for blank status or blank next action date. If more than one or two rows are blank, your routine is slipping.
The promises log

Add a third tab called **Promises** with columns: Date made, Client, What I promised, Due by, Done (Yes or No). Examples: "free hem adjustment on blue gown", "10 percent off next order", "send recipe for zobo". A forgotten promise does more harm than not promising at all, because the client remembers it even if you do not. Sort this tab by Due by every Monday.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A short checklist each month keeps records accurate and promises kept.

blocks.text: Sorting clients by value and engagement

**Value** is how much a client spends with you, using the Total spent column. **Engagement** is how active the relationship is: recent orders, replies, referrals. Split each at a level that makes sense for your business, for example value above or below your average client spend, and engagement as Active or New versus Quiet or Lapsed.

blocks.title: Four client groups
items: Re-engage: high value, low engagement
Protect: high value, high engagement
Maintain lightly: low value, low engagement
Grow: low value, high engagement
axes: Value to the business (low to high)
blocks.caption: Each group needs a different action, so you spend your limited time where it matters most.

head: Group
What it means
Typical action
rows: Spends a lot and stays active
Personal thank-you, early access to new items, check service is still right
Used to spend a lot but has gone quiet
Personal call or voice note asking honestly how things are and if your service still fits
Mention a related item or service that genuinely suits her needs
Occasional general update only if she agreed to receive them

blocks.title: Worked example: a monthly review of eight clients
blocks.context: For example, Zainab does braids and wig revamps from her salon in Kaduna. Her average client spend over the past year is about 40,000 naira (approximate). On the first Saturday of the month she filters her tracker.
steps: Protect (above 40,000 naira, Active): Hauwa 96,000 and Esther 72,000. Action: thank-you voice note and first choice of December appointment slots.
Re-engage (above 40,000 naira, Quiet or Lapsed): Blessing 64,000, last visit 4 months ago against a usual 6 weeks. Action: personal voice note.
Grow (below 40,000 naira, Active): Aisha 18,000 and Mary 22,000, both come monthly for cornrows. Action: mention the wig revamp service since both wear wigs at weekends, as their records show.
Maintain lightly (below 40,000 naira, Lapsed): Joy, Rita and Patience. Action: include them in the next general update only if they agreed to receive updates.
She checks the Promises tab: Esther was promised a free scalp treatment. Zainab books it for her next visit and marks it done afterwards.
blocks.result: In about 30 minutes Zainab has one clear action for each of eight clients, and her most valuable quiet client gets a personal message before she is lost for good.

blocks.text: What to do with what you find

After sorting, update each client's next action and next action date in the tracker straight away, so the review turns into tasks that appear as red rows on the right day. Note the date of the review in a cell at the top of the sheet. Over several months you will see clients move between groups. Movement from Re-engage back to Protect is one of the clearest signs that your relationship work is succeeding, and it makes a strong example for your capstone.

blocks.title: Put it in your calendar
blocks.text: Choose a fixed time, such as the first Saturday morning of each month, and set a repeating event in Google Calendar or your phone calendar. A review that depends on remembering will be skipped in a busy month.

blocks.title: Value is not the only measure
blocks.text: A small client who refers three friends may be more valuable than a big client who never refers. Add a Referrals column to your Clients tab so referrers are not hidden in the low-value groups.

takeaways: Keep a five-point standard: logged in 24 hours, no blanks, factual notes, promises logged, opt-outs respected.
A Promises tab stops commitments being forgotten.
Sort clients into Protect, Re-engage, Grow and Maintain lightly.
Hold a fixed 30-minute review every month.

activity.title: Run your first account review
steps: Add a Promises tab and log every open promise you can find in your chats.
Filter for blank status or next action and fill them in.
Work out your average client spend from the Total spent column.
Place every client into one of the four groups.
Write one action for each group and complete at least one Re-engage or Protect action this week.
activity.evidence: A screenshot or photo of your four groups and the actions chosen, with phone numbers hidden.

lessons.title: Client data privacy, honesty and knowing your capacity
objectives: Explain the main duties the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 places on anyone holding personal data
Apply practical privacy habits to your tracker, WhatsApp and photos
Get consent before sending marketing messages and honour opt-outs
Calculate your weekly capacity and decline or reschedule work honestly

blocks.text: Your tracker holds names, phone numbers, addresses, spending and sometimes personal details your clients shared in trust. Treating that information carefully is both ethical and a legal duty. Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** set up the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** and lays down principles for anyone who collects or uses personal data. Very small businesses may not have formal registration duties, but the principles are good practice for everyone, and clients trust businesses that follow them.
The principles in plain language

items: **Have a fair reason and be open about it:** collect details to serve the client, and tell her what you keep them for.
**Use it only for that purpose:** a number given for delivery should not be added to someone else's marketing list.
**Keep only what you need:** you need her delivery area, not her salary.
**Keep it accurate:** correct wrong details when you notice them.
**Do not keep it forever:** remove details of clients who ask, or who have been inactive for a long time and no longer need to be contacted.
**Keep it secure:** protect it from loss, theft and casual viewing.

blocks.text: The Act also gives people rights over their data, including the right to know what you hold about them and to ask for it to be corrected or deleted. If a client asks, show her what you have and act on her request. For the full text and guidance, see the NDPC website listed in this course's sources.

blocks.name: personal-data
blocks.alt: A person reviewing personal information cards on a screen
blocks.caption: Client details are lent to you in trust; collect only what you need and protect it.

blocks.text: Everyday privacy habits

blocks.title: Privacy habits for small businesses
items: Sheet shared with no one
Two-step verification on
Consent before broadcasts
Blur names in screenshots
Delete on request
blocks.caption: Five habits cover most of the privacy risks a small client list faces.

items: **Broadcast lists:** WhatsApp broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number, which is a sign they agreed to hear from you. Still ask before adding someone: "May I send you our monthly price list?" Note the answer in her record.
**Opt-outs:** if anyone says stop, mark her record "No marketing" that same day.
**Screenshots and testimonials:** never post a client's chat, photo, face, name or number on Status or social media without her clear permission. Blur or crop names and numbers even when she agrees.
**Groups:** do not add clients to WhatsApp groups where other members can see their numbers unless they agree.
**Shared phones:** if family members use your phone, lock WhatsApp and Sheets with a fingerprint or PIN.

blocks.text: Honesty about capacity

Good relationships can create a new risk: more requests than you can handle well. Saying yes to everything leads to late deliveries, rushed work and broken promises, which damage the very relationships you built. Work out your real capacity and use it to decide.

blocks.title: Worked example: a caterer's weekly capacity
blocks.context: For example, Bisi cooks small chops from home in Ibadan. Besides family duties, she has about 30 working hours a week. A standard party order (about 200 pieces) takes her about 5 hours including shopping, frying, packing and delivery.
steps: Maximum orders a week: 30 hours divided by 5 hours = 6 orders.
She keeps 1 order slot free for repeat clients' urgent requests, so she accepts up to 5 new bookings a week.
It is a busy December week: 4 orders are booked and 3 more requests arrive.
She accepts 1 (making 5), keeps the last slot for her Protect clients, and offers the other 2 people the following week.
Her message: "Thank you for thinking of me. This week is fully booked and I do not want to rush your order. I can do it next Tuesday, or I can recommend a caterer I trust."
blocks.result: Bisi keeps her quality and her promises. The clients she turned away were treated with respect and may book her next time.

blocks.text: If something goes wrong

If your phone is stolen or your WhatsApp account is taken over, act quickly. Use another phone to tell your clients on your Status or through a family member's phone that your account may be misused and that you will never ask them to send money to a new account by chat. Ask your network provider to block the SIM and retrieve your number, then re-register WhatsApp on your new phone and turn on two-step verification again. Change your Google password from another device and check which devices are signed in. Clients forgive a stolen phone; they do not forgive silence while someone uses your name to ask them for money.

blocks.title: Treat clients fairly
blocks.text: Giving loyal clients first choice of slots is fair and normal. Quietly delivering lower quality or ignoring messages from smaller clients is not. Every client should get what she was promised, even if some get extra thank-yous.

takeaways: The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 expects fair, limited, accurate, secure use of personal data.
Ask before adding anyone to broadcasts, and honour every opt-out the same day.
Never post client chats, photos or numbers without permission.
Know your weekly capacity and decline or reschedule honestly.

activity.title: Privacy and capacity check
steps: Check the sharing setting on your tracker and your WhatsApp two-step verification.
Add a Marketing consent column (Yes, No, Not asked) and fill it for every client.
Delete any information you hold that you do not need to serve the client.
Calculate your weekly capacity in orders or appointments from your available hours.
Write a polite message you can use when you are fully booked.
activity.evidence: A short note showing your capacity calculation, your fully-booked message and confirmation that the privacy checks are done.

lessons.title: Measuring retention: repeat rate, churn, lifetime value and referrals
objectives: Calculate your repeat client rate from your tracker
Calculate retention and churn rates for a period
Track referrals and the business they bring
Set up a small metrics box in Google Sheets that updates itself

blocks.text: Feeling that clients are happy is not evidence. Numbers from your own records show whether your relationship work is paying off, and they make your capstone and any job application far more convincing. You need only four measures, and your tracker already holds the data.
1. Repeat client rate

**Repeat client rate** is the share of your clients who have ordered more than once. Formula: clients with 2 or more orders divided by total clients, times 100. In Google Sheets, if your Orders count is in column K, use =COUNTIF(K2:K,">=2")/COUNTA(A2:A) and format the cell as a percentage.
2. Retention rate and churn rate

**Retention rate** tells you what share of the clients you had at the start of a period you still have at the end. Use the standard formula: (clients at end of period minus new clients gained during it) divided by clients at start, times 100. **Churn rate** is the opposite: 100 minus retention. Decide what counts as still a client, for example someone who ordered at least once in the period.

blocks.title: Worked example: one quarter's numbers for a soap supplier
blocks.context: For example, Funmi reviews January to March. She counts active clients from her tracker.
steps: Clients at start of January (S): 40.
New clients gained during the quarter (N): 12.
Clients active at end of March (E): 45.
Retention = (45 minus 12) divided by 40 = 33 divided by 40 = 0.825, so 82.5 percent.
Churn = 100 minus 82.5 = 17.5 percent. So 7 of her 40 starting clients did not order in the quarter.
Repeat rate: her list now holds 52 clients (the 40 she started with plus 12 new). 29 of them have 2 or more orders. 29 divided by 52 is about 56 percent.
blocks.result: Funmi now has a baseline. Next quarter she will see whether her reorder reminders and after-care checks raise retention above 82.5 percent.

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.alt: A woman beside a rising bar chart
blocks.caption: Measuring repeat rate and retention each quarter shows whether your relationship work is paying off.

blocks.text: 3. Average lifetime value

You met lifetime value in Lesson 1 as an estimate. Your tracker now gives a real figure for the past: the average of the Total spent column, =AVERAGE(L2:L). Track it each quarter. If it rises while client numbers stay the same, existing clients are buying more, which is direct evidence of stronger relationships.
4. Referrals

Your Source column already shows who came by referral. Count them with =COUNTIF(C2:C,"Referral*") (the star matches anything after the word, such as "Referral by Nkechi"). Then add up what those referred clients have spent. This shows the real value of thanking the people who recommend you.

blocks.title: The relationship pyramid
items: All clients
Repeat clients
Loyal regulars
Active referrers
blocks.caption: Each level is smaller than the one below; your goal is to move more people up a level each quarter.

head: Measure
Formula
Funmi's quarter
rows: Clients with 2+ orders / all clients x 100
Count of Source starting with Referral

blocks.text: Reading the numbers sensibly

Numbers need context. A drop in retention in January may simply follow a busy December, and a rise before Sallah or Christmas may be seasonal. Compare the same quarter across years when you can, or at least note what else was happening. Look at who left, not only how many: losing three small household clients is different from losing your biggest shop. When a number moves, go back to the records and the written feedback to find out why.

items: If repeat rate is low, check the after-care stage and your reorder reminders first.
If retention falls, look at the Re-engage group and call the most valuable clients who left.
If referrals are few, thank existing referrers personally and ask happy Protect clients whether they know anyone who could use your service.
If lifetime value rises while client numbers stay flat, your existing relationships are deepening: protect what is working.

blocks.text: Keep every quarter's figures in one small table at the bottom of your Metrics tab, with the dates beside them. Four or five quarters of honest numbers tell a much clearer story than any single result.

blocks.title: Build a metrics box
blocks.text: Add a small tab called Metrics with the four formulas, each pointing at your Clients tab. Every time you log orders, the numbers update. Write the figures down on the first day of each quarter so you can compare over time.

blocks.title: Do not fool yourself
blocks.text: Count honestly: include clients who left unhappy, and do not move the start date to make the number look better. A modest, true number that improves is far more convincing than a perfect number nobody can check.

takeaways: Repeat rate = clients with 2+ orders / all clients.
Retention = (end minus new) / start; churn = 100 minus retention.
Average Total spent gives a real lifetime value figure.
Count referrals from the Source column and what they spend.

activity.title: Set your baseline numbers
steps: Add a Metrics tab to your tracker.
Enter formulas for repeat rate, average total spent and referral count.
Choose the last three months and count S, N and E by hand from your records.
Calculate retention and churn.
Write the date and all five figures in a notebook or note as your baseline.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Metrics tab and your written retention and churn calculation.

quiz.q: Ada started the quarter with 50 clients, gained 10 new ones and ended with 48 active clients. What is her retention rate?
Hauwa spends a lot but has not booked in four months, against her usual six weeks. Which group is she in, and what should Zainab do?
options: Maintain lightly: include her in a general update
Re-engage: send a personal message asking honestly how things are
quiz.explain: High value with low engagement is the Re-engage group. A personal, honest check-in is the right first step.

quiz.q: A client says, "Please stop sending me your price lists." What should you do?
options: Mark her record No marketing the same day and stop marketing messages
Send one more to remind her of the discounts
Remove her from the list only next month
Delete her number but add it back in December
quiz.explain: Respecting opt-outs immediately is required good practice and protects trust.

quiz.q: Bisi has 24 working hours a week and each order takes 4 hours. What is her maximum number of orders per week?
quiz.explain: 24 divided by 4 = 6 orders. She may also keep one slot free for urgent requests from loyal clients.

quiz.q: A happy client sends a lovely message. Before posting a screenshot of it on your Status, what should you do?
options: Ask her permission and hide her name and number
Post it but delete it after 24 hours
Forward it to all your groups
quiz.explain: Client messages are personal data. Get clear permission and hide identifying details.

quiz.q: Of 30 clients, 18 have ordered two or more times. What is the repeat client rate?

modules.title: Portfolio and impact: your capstone, your case story and your 90-day plan
modules.overview: You will assemble your capstone from real work: a functioning tracker, one proactive relationship action and the client's response. You will learn to turn that work into a short, honest case story with numbers for employers, partners and clients, and finish with a 90-day plan and a weekly routine that keeps your relationships growing after the course.

lessons.title: Building your capstone: tracker, a proactive action and the client's response
objectives: Select the right client for a proactive relationship action
Write a value-first outreach message that is specific to her
Record the action and the client's response as evidence
Prepare evidence that protects client privacy

blocks.text: Your capstone proves that you can manage client relationships, not just describe them. It has three parts: a **functioning tracker** with real client history, **one proactive action** you took with a real client and her response, and a **90-day plan** (Lesson 12). This lesson covers the first two.
Part 1: tracker readiness check

items: At least 10 real clients, each with status and next action date filled in.
Orders tab with at least three months of real orders, and COUNTIF and SUMIF totals working.
Promises tab with open and completed promises.
Metrics tab showing repeat rate, retention, churn and referrals with a dated baseline.
A record of at least one monthly account review with actions for each group.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.alt: A woman presenting a portfolio of her work
blocks.caption: Your capstone is a small portfolio of real evidence: records, an action and a response.

blocks.text: Part 2: choosing the client and the action

Use your monthly review. The best capstone candidates are usually a **Re-engage** client (valuable but gone quiet) or a **Grow** client (active, with a need you noticed). Look at her notes: what has she told you about her business, family events or plans? The action must give her something useful, not simply ask for an order.

head: Weak outreach
Value-first outreach
rows: "Hello, any work for me this month?"
"You mentioned your shop anniversary is on 15 July. Would branded gift packs for your loyal customers help? I can show you two sample designs."
"We have new stock, check my Status"
"The size 16 ankara gowns you asked about in March are back in stock. I kept two aside for you until Friday."
"I noticed your last order was in February. Is the supply still working for your shop, or has something changed I should know about?"

blocks.title: Planning a proactive action
items: Pick client from review
Read her notes
Find a genuine need
Send specific message
Record her response
blocks.caption: A proactive action starts from what you already know about her, which is why the records matter.

blocks.title: Worked example: a designer's proactive action
blocks.context: For example, Tolu is a freelance graphic designer in Abuja. Her client Grace runs a catering business and had a menu designed in January. Tolu's notes from a call say: "Grace said she wants to start taking orders by WhatsApp catalogue but has no good food photos."
steps: In her April review, Grace is in the Grow group: active, but only one small job so far.

Tolu sends: "Hi Grace, you mentioned wanting to use the WhatsApp catalogue. I put together a one-page guide to taking food photos in daylight with a phone. Here it is, free. If you would like, I can also design matching price cards for the catalogue."
Grace replies the same day, thanks her and asks for a quote for 12 price cards.
Tolu quotes 30,000 naira (approximate), Grace agrees, and Tolu logs the order and a new note.
Tolu asks Grace whether she may describe this exchange, without her name, in a course project. Grace agrees.
blocks.result: Tolu's capstone evidence shows the original note, the message, the reply and the new order, all with Grace's consent and her name hidden.

blocks.text: Not every action will lead to an order, and that is fine. A warm reply, a useful conversation or honest feedback about why a client left are all real outcomes. Record exactly what happened. An honest "no order yet, but she shared that prices at a nearer supplier are lower" is better evidence than an invented success.
Part 3: protecting privacy in your evidence

items: Ask the client's permission before using her messages, even with her name hidden.
Crop or blur names, phone numbers, profile photos and addresses in every screenshot.
Replace her name with a label such as "Client A" in your written summary.
Share your tracker as a screenshot or a copy with fake or hidden contact details, never the live file.

blocks.text: Writing the capstone summary

Finish with a half-page written summary that a reviewer can read in two minutes. Use four short headings: **My tracker** (number of clients, tabs, how long you have used it), **My baseline** (the dated metrics from Lesson 9), **My proactive action** (which group the client was in, the note that prompted the action, what you sent, what she replied and what happened next) and **What I learned** (one or two honest sentences, including anything that did not go as planned). Attach the screenshots in the same order so the reviewer can match each claim to its evidence.
If your first choice of client does not reply within a week, do not send repeated messages. Record the silence, choose a second client from the same group, and include both attempts in your summary.

blocks.title: Capture as you go
blocks.text: Take your screenshots on the day you send the message and the day she replies. Trying to rebuild evidence weeks later is slow, and chats get lost when phones change.

takeaways: The capstone has three parts: tracker, one proactive action with its response, and a 90-day plan.
Choose a Re-engage or Grow client and start from her notes.
Value-first messages give something specific before asking for anything.
Ask permission and hide all identifying details in your evidence.

activity.title: Take your capstone action
steps: Complete the tracker readiness check and fix any gaps.
Choose one client from your Re-engage or Grow group and read her notes.
Write a value-first message using a detail from her record, and send it.
Record her response, or lack of response after one week, in her record.
Ask permission to use the exchange anonymously and save privacy-safe screenshots.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your message and her reply with identifying details hidden, plus the updated client record.

lessons.title: Showing the value of your client work with a case story
objectives: Write a short case story using Situation, Action, Result
Present before-and-after numbers honestly
Adapt the story for an employer, a business partner and a client
Explain client relationship skills in an interview for account or client success roles

blocks.text: Saying "I am good with clients" proves nothing; everyone says it. A short case story with real numbers and a real example is what convinces an employer, a business partner or a bigger client. In this lesson you turn your course work into a story you can tell in two minutes or write in half a page.
The SAR structure

items: **Situation:** what was the problem, with a number if possible. "I had 46 clients but no record of who had stopped buying."
**Action:** what you did, specifically. "I built a Google Sheets tracker, set reorder reminders from each client's buying gap, and started day-3 after-care checks."
**Result:** what changed, with before and after figures and the time period. "Over one quarter, retention went from 82.5 percent to 88 percent and three lapsed shop clients returned."

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two women talking across a table in an interview
blocks.caption: A two-minute case story with real numbers is stronger than any claim of being good with people.

blocks.title: Claim versus evidence
items: Vague claim
Case story
blocks.caption: Replace each general claim with a number or a specific action you can show.

blocks.title: Worked example: one case story, three audiences
blocks.context: For example, Funmi has finished the course. Her baseline quarter showed 82.5 percent retention. In the next quarter, after reminders and after-care checks, she started with 45 clients, gained 8 new and ended with 48.
steps: She calculates the new retention: (48 minus 8) divided by 45 = 40 divided by 45 = about 89 percent.

For a job application as a customer success assistant, she writes: "I manage 48 retail and household clients using a Google Sheets CRM I built. By timing reorder reminders to each client's buying gap, I raised quarterly retention from 82.5 percent to about 89 percent."
For a possible distribution partner, she leads with reliability: "My shop clients reorder about every 29 days and I have not missed a delivery date this quarter."
For a new shop client, she keeps it simple: "I keep a record of every shop's usual order and remind you before you run out, so you are never without stock."
blocks.result: One honest set of numbers becomes three short messages, each matched to what that reader cares about.

blocks.text: Before-and-after tables

head: Measure
Before (baseline quarter)
After (next quarter)
rows: Clients with a next action date

blocks.title: Honesty rules
blocks.text: Use only numbers you can show from your records. Say what period they cover. Do not claim your methods caused every improvement: prices, season and the economy also play a part. "Retention rose while I introduced reminders" is honest; "my reminders guaranteed 89 percent retention" is not.
Roles where these skills matter

Job titles that rely heavily on this work include **account manager**, **client success** or **customer success** associate, **relationship officer** (common in Nigerian banks and microfinance), and **client service executive** in agencies. In interviews you may be asked, "Tell me about a time you kept a client from leaving." Answer with your SAR story, mention the tool you used, and be ready to explain one formula, such as how you calculated retention.
Answering common interview questions

head: Question
What a strong answer includes
rows: Tell me about a time you kept a client from leaving.
A Re-engage client from your review, the warning signals you saw, the message you sent and the result.
How do you keep track of many clients?
Your Clients, Orders and Promises tabs, the overdue highlight and your weekly 30-minute routine.
How do you handle a client who wants more than you can deliver?
Your capacity calculation and an honest message that offers a later date or a trusted alternative.
How do you measure whether clients are happy?
Repeat rate, retention, NPS with written comments, and one change you made because of feedback.

blocks.text: If you have worked only for yourself, that still counts. Running your own client list for months is direct experience of account management. Say so plainly and show your tracker screenshots with contact details hidden. If you are asked about a CRM you have not used, such as Salesforce or HubSpot, be honest, explain that you built and ran your own system in Google Sheets, and say you are ready to learn theirs. Employers usually care more that you understand records, follow-up and measurement than which software you used.
Keep your case story up to date. Each quarter, replace the Result line with your newest figures, so you always have a current, checkable example ready when an opportunity comes.

blocks.title: Practise out loud
blocks.text: Record yourself telling your case story as a WhatsApp voice note to yourself. Aim for under two minutes. Listen back and cut anything that is not Situation, Action or Result.

takeaways: Use Situation, Action, Result, with real numbers and a time period.
Replace general claims with figures or specific actions.
Adjust the same facts for employers, partners and clients.
Never claim more than your records show.

activity.title: Write your case story
steps: Write your Situation in one or two sentences with a number.
Write your Action naming the tracker, the rhythm and the review you set up.
Write your Result using your baseline and your latest figures, with dates.
Make a short version for an employer and another for a client.
Record a voice note of the employer version in under two minutes.
activity.evidence: Your written SAR case story in both versions and the voice note.

lessons.title: Your 90-day relationship plan, weekly routine and certification checklist
objectives: Write a 90-day plan that names one relationship to deepen and a communication rhythm
Block a weekly CRM time in your calendar
Set measurable 90-day targets from your baseline
Check your capstone evidence is complete before certification

blocks.text: Relationship management is not a project you finish. It is a routine. The goal of this final lesson is to make your new habits automatic, with a plan for the next 90 days and a fixed weekly time in your calendar, so that the work continues when the course is over and business gets busy.
The weekly 30-minute routine

items: Open the tracker and filter for red rows (overdue next actions). Act on each or reschedule it with a reason.
Log any orders from the week that are not yet entered.
Check the Promises tab for anything due in the next seven days.
Send after-care checks for this week's deliveries.
Send reorder reminders for clients near the end of their usual gap.

blocks.name: spiral-calendar-pad
blocks.caption: A fixed weekly slot in your calendar turns good intentions into a habit.

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: A 90-day relationship plan
items: Weeks 1 to 2: clean records
Weeks 3 to 6: build rhythm
Week 6: mid-point review
Weeks 7 to 12: deepen
Day 90: measure and reset
blocks.caption: Each phase builds on the one before, ending with numbers you can compare to your baseline.

blocks.text: Your plan must name **one specific relationship to deepen** and **a communication rhythm** you will keep. It should also set two or three targets based on the baseline you recorded in Lesson 9. Targets should be modest and measurable: a few percentage points better retention, a set number of after-care checks, one referral a month.

blocks.title: Worked example: Zainab's 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Zainab, the salon owner in Kaduna, recorded a baseline of 70 percent retention, 4 referred clients and no after-care checks. She writes her plan on 1 October.
steps: Relationship to deepen: Blessing, a high-value client in the Re-engage group. Action: personal voice note in week 1, then offer her a fixed fortnightly slot that suits her work hours.
Communication rhythm: day-3 after-care message for every client; monthly style tips to clients who agreed; reorder reminders 5 days before each client's usual gap ends.
Weekly routine: Saturdays 7:30 to 8:00 am, blocked in Google Calendar as a repeating event.
Targets for 31 December: retention 75 percent or more; after-care check sent after 90 percent of appointments; at least 3 new referred clients.
Mid-point check in mid-November: if after-care checks are below 90 percent, she saves the message as a quick reply to make it faster.
blocks.result: Zainab's plan is specific enough that anyone could check on 31 December whether she did it.

blocks.text: Certification checklist

head: Evidence
Done when
rows: 10+ real clients, status and next action for each, Orders and Promises tabs in use
Repeat rate, retention, churn and referrals recorded with a date
Message, client response and updated record, privacy-safe
SAR story with real numbers in employer and client versions
One named relationship, a rhythm, weekly time block, 2 to 3 targets
Ten-point audit from Lesson 3 repeated and compared with your first score

blocks.text: When the plan slips

Every plan meets a bad week: illness, a family event, a power cut that lasts days, a sudden rush of orders. Decide now what your minimum routine is when time is short, for example only clearing red rows and logging orders, which takes about ten minutes. Missing one week is normal; missing four in a row means the routine needs to change, perhaps to a different day or a shorter list. At the mid-point review, be honest about which parts of the plan you are actually doing, and cut or simplify the rest rather than abandoning everything.

items: Minimum routine (10 minutes): clear red rows, log new orders.
Normal routine (30 minutes): add promises check, after-care messages and reorder reminders.
Monthly (30 minutes more): account review and group actions.
Quarterly (1 hour): update metrics, compare with baseline, adjust targets.

blocks.text: Finally, share your plan with one person you trust, such as a fellow WODDI learner, a business partner or a family member, and ask her to check on you at the mid-point and at day 90. Telling someone makes it more likely you will follow through. When day 90 arrives, update your metrics, compare them with your baseline, write a new case story Result line, and set the next 90-day plan. That repeating cycle is what turns a course into a lasting business habit.

blocks.title: Re-take the audit
blocks.text: Go back to the ten-point audit from Lesson 3 and answer it again. Most learners who complete the activities move several points. Write both scores side by side; this simple comparison is strong evidence of change.

blocks.title: Where to go next
blocks.text: If your client list grows past a few hundred, or you employ staff who need shared access, explore a free CRM plan such as HubSpot or Zoho. You can import your Google Sheets data as a CSV file, so nothing you built here is wasted.

takeaways: A fixed weekly 30-minute review keeps the system alive.
The 90-day plan names one relationship, one rhythm and 2 to 3 measurable targets.
Use your Lesson 9 baseline to set realistic targets.
Re-take the audit and complete the checklist before certification.

activity.title: Commit to your next 90 days
steps: Create a repeating weekly 30-minute event in your calendar for client review.
Write your 90-day plan with one named relationship, your rhythm and 2 to 3 targets.
Set a mid-point review date in your calendar.
Re-take the ten-point audit and record both scores.
Tick off every item on the certification checklist.
activity.evidence: Your written 90-day plan, a screenshot of the calendar event, and your before and after audit scores.

quiz.q: Which outreach message is the best value-first proactive action?
options: "Please check my Status for new stock."
"You mentioned your shop anniversary on 15 July. Would gift packs for your loyal customers help? I can show two samples."
quiz.explain: It uses a specific detail from her record and offers something useful to her, rather than just asking for work.

quiz.q: Funmi started a quarter with 45 clients, gained 8 new ones and ended with 48. What was her retention rate?
quiz.explain: (48 minus 8) / 45 = 40 / 45, which is about 89%.

quiz.q: Which sentence is an honest Result statement?
options: My reminders caused all my growth
Retention rose from 82.5% to about 89% over one quarter while I introduced reorder reminders
quiz.explain: It uses real numbers, a time period and does not claim more than the records show.

quiz.q: Your proactive message got no order, but the client explained she found a cheaper supplier nearer her shop. How should you record this for your capstone?
options: Leave it out and try someone else
Record exactly what happened; it is genuine, useful evidence
Say she placed a small order
Ask a friend to pretend to be a client
quiz.explain: Honest outcomes, including learning why a client left, are real evidence. Inventing results is dishonest.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in a 90-day plan according to this course?
options: One named relationship to deepen and a communication rhythm
A promise to message every client daily
A plan to buy expensive CRM software
A list of clients' personal secrets
quiz.explain: The plan names one relationship, a rhythm, a weekly time block and 2 to 3 measurable targets.

quiz.q: Before using a client's chat in your capstone evidence, what must you do?
options: Ask her permission and hide her name, number and photo
quiz.explain: Client messages are personal data. Consent and hiding identifying details protect her privacy.

finalQuiz.q: A hairdresser's clients spend about 15,000 naira per visit, visit 8 times a year and stay about 3 years. What is the estimated client lifetime value?
Which of these is the best note for a client record?
options: 7 Sept: asked for delivery after 4pm on weekdays; shop closes at 7pm
finalQuiz.explain: Useful notes are dated, factual and tell you how to serve her next time.

finalQuiz.q: Halima ordered on 1 Jan, 31 Jan, 2 Mar and 1 Apr. About when should Funmi send the next reorder reminder?
finalQuiz.explain: 1 Jan to 1 Apr is 90 days over 3 gaps, about 30 days. A reminder a few days before 1 May, around 27 April, is right.

finalQuiz.q: In Google Sheets, what does =SUMIF(Orders!B:B,A2,Orders!D:D) give you?
options: The total amount spent by the client named in A2
The date of her last order
finalQuiz.explain: SUMIF adds the amounts in column D only where column B matches the client in A2.

finalQuiz.q: A long-standing client's orders are getting smaller and she has not replied to your last three messages. What is the best next step?
options: Send daily promotions until she replies
Send one honest, personal check-in asking whether your service still fits her needs
finalQuiz.explain: Two warning signals together call for a gentle, honest check-in, not pressure or panic discounting.

finalQuiz.q: Of 25 parents asked the 0 to 10 question, 15 give 9 or 10, 6 give 7 or 8 and 4 give 6 or less. What is the NPS?
Why keep a separate Promises tab in your tracker?
options: So no discount, free service or date you agreed is forgotten
finalQuiz.explain: A forgotten promise damages trust. Logging and reviewing promises keeps you consistent.

finalQuiz.q: A client spends well above average but has not ordered for twice her usual gap. Which group is she in?
finalQuiz.explain: High value with low engagement is the Re-engage group, which deserves a personal message.

finalQuiz.q: Which practice best fits the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 principles for a small business?
options: Collect as many personal details as possible in case they are useful
Share your client sheet with 'Anyone with the link' for convenience
Collect only what you need, keep it secure, and correct or delete it when a client asks
Post client chats as testimonials without asking
finalQuiz.explain: The Act's principles include purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, security and respecting people's rights over their data.

finalQuiz.q: Ngozi has 35 working hours a week, each cake order takes 7 hours, and she keeps one slot for loyal clients. How many new bookings should she accept per week?
finalQuiz.explain: 35 / 7 = 5 orders maximum. Keeping one slot free leaves 4 for new bookings.

finalQuiz.q: A quarter starts with 60 clients, 15 new ones join, and 63 are active at the end. What are retention and churn?
Which is the strongest way to show an employer your client relationship skills?
options: Say you are a people person
Promise you will never lose a client
Tell a short Situation, Action, Result story with real before-and-after numbers
finalQuiz.explain: A SAR story with real, dated numbers is specific and checkable, unlike general claims.

Record your baseline: repeat rate, retention, churn, referrals and your ten-point audit score.
Run a monthly account review and place every client in Protect, Re-engage, Grow or Maintain lightly.

Write your SAR case story in an employer version and a client version.
Write your 90-day plan with one named relationship, a communication rhythm, a weekly time block and 2 to 3 targets.
